The M67 has been closed in both directions on weeknights between 20:00 and 06:00 since July and lorries and cars will continue to be diverted onto Mottram Road, in Godley, Tameside, until December. National Highways said it "understands" the impact roadworks can have on local people. Image caption, Work is taking place at the M67 Junction 4 roundabout as part of the Mottram bypass scheme Image caption, John Sullivan said HGVs should be directed away from Mottram Road when the M67 is closed John Sullivan said: "You can't relax in your own home and you can't sleep at night because you're waiting for the next lorry." On one night when the M67 was closed, the couple say they counted 758 HGVs and 4,609 cars passing their home in Godley between 20:00 and 06:00. The couple have also urged Tameside Council to resurface Mottram Road and impose a reduced speed limit to minimise noise. title: What does Wythenshawe mean to the people who know it best?

input.lead: As Wythenshawe marks its centenary, 100 people tell the BBC what it is really like to live and work there
input.summary: As Wythenshawe marks its centenary, 100 people tell the BBC what it is really like to live and work there
input.evidence_text: This year marks 100 years since Wythenshawe Hall was donated to Manchester Corporation At the time, the city was in urgent need of more housing In 1920 an urban planner called Patrick Abercrombie identified Wythenshawe as the only undeveloped land suitable for building a housing estate close to Manchester To turn his proposal into a reality, Ernest and Shena Simon bought Wythenshawe Hall from Robert Henry Grenville Tatton in 1926, which they donated to the city's corporation (now known as the council) The idea was that people could be rehoused away from industrial Manchester into what became known as the "Garden City" To celebrate 100 years, BBC North West Tonight has spoken to 100 people from the area about what Wythenshawe means to them

Situated on a council estate in the Wythenshawe area of Manchester, people travelled from far and wide to enjoy shows at the 1,400-capacity venue. From music stars Dusty Springfield, Roy Orbison and Eartha Kitt to comedians Tommy Cooper and Ronnie Corbett, there was never a shortage of acts wanting to appear. "I think Dusty Springfield was the big highlight for me," said 79-year-old John Orchard, who was a pianist for Shep's Banjo Boys from 1969 to 1972. "She was my favourite singer in the 1960s and all of a sudden there she is at the Golden Garter. "This is a nightclub in Wythenshawe under the flight path of the Ringway airport (now known as Manchester Airport) in the middle of the biggest council estate in Europe. "So it was a bit incongruous, but it was a fantastic place and Wythenshawe loved it and it loved Wythenshawe." Image source, Unknown Image caption, The Golden Garter could pack in crowds of up to 1,400 The Golden Garter holds many happy memories for Paul Stoloff, who was a bassist for the Golden Garter Showband from 1970 to 1982. "It was good fun - happy times," he said. "It was interesting because it was different music every week. "So if you didn't like what they're doing, it'd be different for the next week." title: Intercompany transactions: five examples explained | About Manchester

input.lead: A £900 sale between two subsidiaries is revenue for the seller, yet contributes no external revenue to the group.
input.summary: A £900 sale between two subsidiaries is revenue for the seller, yet contributes no external revenue to the group. The difference lies in whose accounts you are reading. Intercompany transactions are exchanges between separate companies within a corporate group, including a parent
input.evidence_text: A £900 sale between two subsidiaries is revenue for the seller, yet contributes no external revenue to the group. The difference lies in whose accounts you are reading Intercompany transactions are exchanges between separate companies within a corporate group, including a parent and subsidiary or two subsidiaries. Each records its own side of the transaction; consolidated accounts present the included companies as one economic entity. A charge These illustrative examples assume wholly owned companies included in the same consolidation and set aside tax, currency and impairment effects Company A buys stock from an external supplier for £600, then sells it to Company B for £900. A records £900 revenue and £600 cost of sales; B records £900 inventory At group level, the internal sale is eliminated from revenue. Finance teams can use financial consolidation software to support that process, working from records that identify the other company and transaction amount Suppose all the stock remains unsold to external customers at the reporting date. B’s £900 inventory includes £300 profit made inside the group. Eliminating this unrealised profit reduces group inventory to its original £600 cost and removes the internal gain from group profit

title: Is the funding market getting harder and what could that mean for Manchester? | Manchester Digital

input.lead: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing.
input.summary: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised
input.evidence_text: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised. More capital is being concentrated in fewer companies while the market for exits remains difficult Financial news recently added another dimension to that discussion. AI-related shares fell last week after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slower approach to the development of increasingly capable AI models. Nvidia finished the day down 3.4%, SoftBank fell 10.7% in Tokyo Additionally, the Bank of England is predicted to increase interest rates later this year, which could affect the North West's tech funding landscape by raising the cost of capital across the board, compressing valuations, pushing investors toward profitability over growth-at-all The British Business Bank's 2026 Small Business Equity Tracker found that equity investment into UK smaller businesses fell 4% to £12.3bn in 2025. Seed deal numbers fell 27% and venture deals fell 13%. AI companies attracted 44% of all investment into smaller businesses while the Beauhurst recorded £14.4bn of UK equity investment across 2,799 deals in the first half of 2026 but three AI companies accounted for 29% of all the capital raised. Those very large rounds can make the overall market look stronger than it feels to businesses raising at seed or Ser Beauhurst's analysis shows that UK equity investment more than doubled between 2017 and 2021 to £32.2bn while annual exits remained at around 400 to 500. An exit takes a median of four years from a funding round

But the images he returned with told a more complex story: shot in colour, they showed humanity and dignity alongside the hardship Sixty years later, photographer Simon Hill has retraced that journey. The conversation between their two bodies of work, now showing together at Jodrell Bank, builds a portrait of how much has changed since then and how much remains While Bulmer visited 16 locations across the North, Hill travelled to more than 50. From late 2024 to mid 2026 he crossed the historic seven counties from Newcastle to Liverpool, visiting former mining communities, coastal towns, city centres, remote landscapes, and the motorways In homage to Bulmer’s pioneering use of colour, much of Hill’s work was shot on Harman Phoenix 200, a contemporary colour film made in the North, and known for its unpredictable, textured qualities Bulmer’s North captured communities facing uncertain futures as the industries that defined them began to disappear. Hill’s is post-industrial, more diverse and still evolving. Former centres of heavy industry have become sites of cultural reinvention and technological growth. Bu Jodrell Bank feels a particularly fitting setting for work that’s fundamentally about time, distance and how we measure change. input.evidence_text: Bolton Car Boot Sale is one of the North West's biggest weekly boot sales, held in the hardstanding car park of the Macron Stadium (formerly Reebok), Burnden Way, Horwich, Bolton BL6 6JW. Sellers can arrive and set up from 6:00 AM, with buyers welcomed in from 7:00 AM. Entry costs just £1 per car for buyers. Pitches for sellers are £14 for a car, £20 for a van and £3 for a trailer, with regular and corner pitches available on request. Bring exact change to keep the queue moving, and call organiser Andrew on 07470784644 for more details. Expect hundreds of stalls across the concrete hardstanding pitches, so it goes ahead in most weather. On-site you'll find a 5-star catering service, doughnuts and coffee, ice cream and desserts, a meat auction, fresh fruit and veg, plants, and retro sweet stalls. The sale is dog-friendly, has male and female toilets, ample parking, and kids' rides and bouncy castles to keep little ones entertained. input.evidence_text: 43 years on from our only participation in the European Cup – a first-round defeat to Fenerbahce in 1968 – we qualified for the Champions League for the 2011/12 season. Now, as we approach our 150th game in this historic competition when we take on AEK Athens on Tuesday, we can say the Champions League has more than delivered on its guarantee of joy, heartbreak and everything in between. Having qualified for the continent’s hallmark cup competition in every season since Roberto Mancini led us there in 2011, we are currently on the longest ongoing run of appearances in the Champions League of any English side. The level of consistency required not to miss out in all that time speaks volumes to our domestic dominance particularly under Pep Guardiola but also with Mancini and Manuel Pellegrini. We have, after all, won the Premier League more than every other club combined since that 2011/12 season began. However, it’s not always been the same in Europe. With the finest of margins often deciding knockout ties between the most talented players on the planet, it felt for a long time as if City were destined never to lift the famous old trophy with the giant ear-shaped handles. That all changed in 2023, when Rodri curled home against Inter in Istanbul and Ederson produced a last-minute diving save to set the seal on a historic Treble. City had more than deserved it, having swept aside German champions Bayern Munich and defending winners Real Madrid in the previous rounds. But what you deserve isn’t always what you get in the Champions League. Bernardo Silva, who left City in the summer as our joint-most decorated player having been integral to all the successes under Guardiola, said this in his final interview with the club: “I think more of our teams could have done the same.
